item.title: Educators warn AI debate has focused too much on cheating, not enough on student learning
item.description: A Georgia Tech professor said some students are "learning absolutely nothing" as educators rethink assessments with handwritten exams in the AI era.
item.content:encoded:
As the world scrambles to understand and use generative artificial intelligence in a variety of areas, the discourse about its implementation in higher education often centers around plagiarism and cheating. However, educators who spoke to Fox News Digital warned that the public is missing the point. 

They argue that the real issue is determining what students have learned.

"I don't think cheating is the right concept to use here," Georgia Institute of Technology Regents’ Professor and Senior Associate Chair in the School of Interactive Computing Amy Bruckman told Fox News Digital. "I am not commenting on whether I think AI should be in the workplace. I'm simply saying, it seems like it will be, and therefore, banning students from using it at the university level seems like burying your head in the sand."

CHRISTIAN UNIVERSITY AIMS TO PRODUCE 'IRREPLACEABLE' GRADUATES AS AI RESHAPES HIGHER EDUCATION

Bruckman argued that in order for universities to work with students learning in the age of AI, they must redesign what they are teaching in order to help students learn through using AI. However, Bruckman said that rather than taking advantage of technology to further their education, students are "avoiding learning" by using AI.

"Some of the current students are learning absolutely nothing in school," she said.

To understand what their students have actually learned, some professors have resorted to traditional methods of evaluation, such as handwritten exams that eliminate the possibility of relying on AI.

Bruckman told Fox News Digital that she is among the educators returning to analog evaluations by giving closed-book tests on paper to ensure that she is actually seeing what her students know. She said that this model separates students who used AI to complete their assignments without taking in the information from those who actually engaged with the content.

"I think we have to redesign our assessments to be resistant to AI," she said. "To say, 'I don't care whether you used AI or not, I'm going to give you a test that shows whether you learned the content that was part of the learning objectives.'"

CALIFORNIA PROFESSOR ARGUES NEED FOR 'OBJECTIVE MEASURES' AFTER STATE DROPS ACT/SAT REQUIREMENT

The Georgia Tech professor is not alone in rethinking how student learning is evaluated. Several educators are not pushing for a ban on AI, but for changes so they can truly evaluate students' understanding of the material.

Generations College Chancellor Dr. Grace Alexis told Fox News Digital that many faculty members initially viewed AI through the lens of potential cheating and plagiarism before realizing that they needed to rethink how to use the revolutionary technology in the classroom. Alexis said that this happened at her own institution and that instructors had not only learned how to use AI, but how to train students to use it in a way that enhances their critical thinking skills.

Alexis argued that the challenge is not simply allowing students to use AI, but ensuring that they do not end up relying on it. She compared it to the way previous generations used encyclopedias, noting that AI could be used to inform students' work without doing it for them.

"It's important for our students to understand that it is OK to use AI in the classroom ... It's really up to the faculty members to not only embrace the technology, but help their students embrace it properly and train them how to do that," she said.

While both educators who spoke to Fox News Digital agree that AI should be incorporated rather than banned outright, they warned that students still need to develop the critical-thinking skills that higher education is meant to cultivate.

"The students in my class fall into two groups," she explained. "The bottom half are definitely losing their critical thinking skills. I would not hire them to feed my cat, and I do not have a cat."

She said the other half of her students are still engaging with the material and are working to learn, adding that "we're not losing everyone, but we're losing a good chunk."

WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL

Despite her concerns about the risks of generative AI use, Bruckman said that she has no interest in becoming an "AI cop." She recognized that despite whatever skepticism higher education has about AI, their students will need to use it when they enter the workforce.

"I don't want to waste my whole semester accusing people of AI use when they're going to need AI in their jobs," she said. "Teaching them appropriate use and redesigning assignments so that they can learn while using whatever tools they have at their disposal, I think, is the only way to go."

Bruckman believes that higher education will eventually adapt to AI, but she remains concerned that students will be lost during the transition.

"We will meet this challenge," she said. "My concern is that we will lose a generation of students in the gap while we're figuring it out."

item.title: 'Baywatch' star Brandy Ledford shares fitness secrets at 57, says she's 'not ready to hang up my bikini yet'
item.description: Brandy Ledford reveals her fitness routine now centers on heavy weight training for bone density and shares the beauty secrets behind her ageless look.
item.content:encoded:
Brandy Ledford has no problem revealing the secrets behind her youthful glow.

The "Baywatch: Hawaii" alum said her beauty routine boils down to two Bs: "Botox and bleach."

The star, 57, who made hearts race as lifeguard Dawn Masterton, is hosting a luxury wellness retreat for women in September. She is also a creator on Passes, where she shares exclusive content and connects directly with fans.

JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'

Ledford told Fox News Digital that she has zero qualms about still being recognized as a sex symbol by fans today.

"I love, I mean, I'm a grandmother," she gushed. "I mean, what? That's so great! I think it's so fun. I'm not ready to hang up my bikini yet."

As she has gotten older, Ledford said her fitness philosophy has evolved.

"My fitness routine these days focuses on strength training more than ever," she said. "When you get to be my age, you need to lift weights for bone density and longevity. My doctor is really stressing weight training using heavier weights for me."

WATCH: ‘BAYWATCH: HAWAII’ ALUM BRANDY LEDFORD REVEALS HER FITNESS SECRETS

"For the last few years, I was pretty addicted to yoga sculpt, a high-intensity yoga workout with light weights. I'm really trying to use much heavier weights now to strengthen my bones and muscles."

"I also still love walking, and I still love yoga," Ledford said. "I love to go on hikes. But I'd say right now, I'm really, really, really focused on serious weight training."

Ledford's commitment to fitness is not new. Looking back, she said landing "Baywatch" required her to kick one unhealthy habit.

WATCH: ‘BAYWATCH’ STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SAYS FAITH HELPED TRANSFORM HER SOBRIETY JOURNEY

"I'm a really good swimmer," she said. "I'm from the beach, so we grew up swimming in the ocean. But at the time, I was a smoker, and there were stamina tests. They would throw quarters to the bottom of the deep end of the pool, and you'd have to swim down. They wanted to see how long you could hold your breath. It was kind of hard for me at the time, so I quit smoking."

"I did end up getting a lot better at holding my breath underwater and became a lot better at swimming," she added.

Ledford also "hired a trainer immediately" to make sure she always looked swimsuit-ready for every scene.

"He trained me in the water and got me really comfortable working and exercising in the water," she said. "Then I worked out with weights. I also did a lot of workouts in the sand. The sand is an incredible workout. Even walking in the sand is a great workout. And when we got to Hawaii, we worked out at the gym there."

"I just trained a lot," she said. "I really wanted to be comfortable in my swimsuit and not be self-conscious. I think that shows. When you're self-conscious, it shows. So I wanted to feel comfortable, and the only way I knew how was to work out and take care of my body."

"We all made it a priority to get our workouts in and swim in the ocean. Walking from our trailer to the set in the sand was a workout in itself. That was really important to me, and it became part of my lifestyle. I've actually maintained it to this day."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Ledford noted she still works out daily to look and feel her best.

"I think health is our greatest wealth," Ledford said. "I really believe that what you feel on the inside is going to come out on the outside. I've been sober for 14 years, and that's been a big life changer. I have a really strong faith in God. Listen, I do all the things, but it starts from the inside. I love really good skincare. I think healthy hair is a big part of it. And I think a beautiful smile is important. I'm always drinking water."

The actress said maintaining her appearance involves more than workouts and beauty treatments.

"I value what I look like on the outside because I value so much of the work I do on the inside," Ledford said. "I always say I do so much work in my inner life. The second I get up, I'm in prayer and meditation. I want to look as good on the outside as I feel on the inside, so I make it a priority. But I'm just as comfortable with no makeup, sweats, a hoodie and my fluffy slippers."

Ledford said she's feeling so good these days that she's even tempted to pull out her "Baywatch" swimsuit and rock it again.

"It's in storage somewhere," she said. "I might pull it out and do a photo shoot in it. It was pretty iconic — yellow — because red is what's known as the 'Baywatch' one-piece. But in 'Baywatch: Hawaii,' we wore yellow because it came from the Australian lifeguards. They wear yellow. It's not an easy color to pull off, but we had so much body makeup on that it all looked good."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Ledford said she's excited to check out the new "Baywatch" reboot, which stars Brooks Nader, Shay Mitchell and Livvy Dunne, among others.

"The advice I'd give the ladies to look glamorous and effortless on the beach in all those scenes is to stay hydrated, wear sunscreen, work out and feel comfortable in your body. They're all so beautiful, fit and in great shape. Every one of those girls looks amazing."

"I think we tend to look back at our younger selves and say, 'I wish I'd known how cute I was. I wish I'd realized I looked good in that bikini.' So just know that you look amazing and let it shine from the inside."

Ledford said she isn't surprised "Baywatch" is still making a splash decades later.

"First of all, it's iconic," she said. "It's a fantasy. People got to escape. The men were hot, and the women were beautiful. But there was also drama and really good action. It was just the perfect show. I think we need that in our lives again these days."

item.title: Nearly 2,000 ocean rescues occur as dangerous surf slams popular beaches this summer
item.description: Nearly 2,000 ocean rescues in one weekend are prompting health and water safety experts to warn about El Niño-driven swells and strong rip currents at beaches.
item.content:encoded:
A 10-year-old boy was standing in ankle-deep water at a California beach recently when he lost his footing and was pulled into the ocean by powerful surf.

Ryder Williams, a 16-year-old California State Parks lifeguard, radioed for help and raced into the water at Seabright State Beach in Santa Cruz during the July 25 emergency, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

The lifeguard's dramatic and widely hailed rescue of the boy — including by President Donald J. Trump, who invited the "heroic young man" and his family to the White House to be recognized — came during a weekend of extremely hazardous conditions along the California coast.

TEXAS TEEN BITTEN BY BARRACUDA IN POPULAR VACATION SPOT AFTER BRACELET GLINTS IN WATER

Hundreds of miles south, Los Angeles County lifeguards performed nearly 2,000 ocean rescues as extreme heat sent large crowds to the beaches, according to the Los Angeles County Lifeguard Division.

Water safety experts interviewed by Fox News Digital are urging beachgoers to take extra precautions as elevated surf and strong rip currents continue to affect portions of the Southern California coast, according to the National Weather Service.    

The Los Angeles County Lifeguard Division shared the rescue totals in an Instagram post, urging visitors to remain vigilant and speak with an on-duty lifeguard before entering the water.

"In total, @lacolifeguards performed just under 2,000 rescues as millions flocked to Los Angeles County beaches to beat the heat," the Instagram post read.

SHARK WEEK DANGERS HIT HOME AS MAN IS BADLY BITTEN WHILE SAVING PREGNANT FIANCÉE FROM HARM

"With a heat advisory continuing across the Southland and a Southern Hemisphere swell expected to keep surf elevated throughout the week, we encourage everyone to take proper precaution, and talk to a lifeguard about conditions before entering the water," officials said in the post.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Los Angeles County Fire Department, which oversees the Los Angeles County Lifeguard Division, for additional comment.

Swells from Hurricane Fausto affected Southern California during the rescue weekend and were expected to produce life-threatening surf and rip currents, according to the National Hurricane Center.

A later swell from Tropical Cyclone Genevieve was expected to bring high surf to Los Angeles and Ventura County beaches through Saturday, the National Weather Service said.

ANGRY CRUISE PASSENGERS BLAST MAJOR LINE OVER SURPRISE DAILY GRATUITY HIKE

The agency warned of very strong rip and longshore currents.

The conditions should not be viewed as a one-time event, said Dr. Molly O’Shea, a Detroit-based pediatrician with Goldfish Swim School.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center said El Niño is expected to strengthen.

O’Shea said the El Niño pattern, combined with swells, could produce elevated surf throughout the summer.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"That combination can keep surf elevated on and off for weeks at a time," she told Fox News Digital.

O’Shea recommended that people swim near an open lifeguard tower and ask a lifeguard about the conditions before entering the water.

Also, "if you see someone struggling, don’t swim out after them without something that floats," she added.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Throw it, don’t go — a lot of rip current deaths are bystanders who tried to help and got caught themselves."

The National Weather Service advises beachgoers to seek out a lifeguard or call 911 when someone is caught in a rip current. A flotation device should be thrown to the person when possible, and would-be rescuers should not enter the water without flotation equipment, according to the agency.

When caught in a rip current, swimmers should remain calm and avoid attempting to swim directly against it, O’Shea said.

"Panic makes people swim as hard as they can against it, and that’s exactly backwards — you’ll exhaust yourself before you get anywhere," she said.

"The move is to relax, swim parallel to the beach until you’re out of the current, then let the waves angle you back in."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Similarly, the National Weather Service advises swimmers caught in a rip current to move parallel to the shoreline until they escape its pull, then swim at an angle toward shore. Those who can't escape should float or tread water and signal for help, according to the agency.

Thomas Gill, president of the United States Lifesaving Association, urged beachgoers not to turn their backs on the ocean.

Gill, based in Virginia, told Fox News Digital that swimmers should "not overestimate [their] ability to handle rough conditions."

"The larger surf leads to more opportunity for strong rip currents," he said.

Rescue events, he added, "are not as uncommon as they seem," particularly during periods of dangerous surf.

item.title: Bipartisan pair of senators urge Rubio to release aid to African women, children at risk of Ebola
item.description: Sens. Jeanne Shaheen and Lisa Murkowski urge Marco Rubio to release $608 million in family planning funds as Ebola ravages the DRC and Uganda.
item.content:encoded:
Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., are urging the State Department to release hundreds of millions of dollars in aid to help women and infants affected by an Ebola outbreak in East Africa.

In a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday, the senators urged him to use $608 million in congressionally-approved international family-planning funds and distribute $1.7 million in already purchased family-planning supplies.

The supplies — which the senators implied included condoms, hormonal contraception, post-rape care medicine and hemorrhage medicines — are being stored at a facility in Geel, Belgium, according to the letter.

The senators said that if the supplies aren't used, their understanding is that they will be "destroyed."

EBOLA TREATMENT CENTER SET ON FIRE IN CONGO AFTER RESIDENTS CLASH WITH AUTHORITIES OVER VICTIM'S BODY

"Ebola during pregnancy is catastrophic, with a nearly 100 percent fetal loss rate and catastrophic material mortality risk due to severe hemorrhaging," the lawmakers wrote.

"By providing women with the option to voluntarily prevent unplanned pregnancies and to protect themselves from transmission of the virus and have access to clinics, the United States can prevent further deaths of women and the cruel and certain death of any fetus exposed to the virus," they added.

The senators also asked the State Department to issue a "humanitarian exception" to support the United Nations Population Fund's existing health clinics in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

SUDAN'S FORGOTTEN WAR LEAVES MILLIONS HUNGRY AS GLOBAL ATTENTION REMAINS ELSEWHERE

As of July 29, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) had reported 3,532 Ebola cases in the DRC and 1,556 deaths, representing a mortality rate of roughly 44%.

In neighboring Uganda, there have been 20 confirmed cases and two deaths, according to the CDC.

Murkowski and Shaheen told the State Department that the virus's rapid spread "leaves no time for delay in providing all possible interventions to save lives."

VACATION HOT SPOT FACES NEW CDC TRAVEL WARNING AS OUTBREAK CASES CONTINUE CLIMBING

"The cost of [the] United States response is approaching $1 billion," they wrote. "Investment now in voluntary family planning is fiscally rational in addition to being morally urgent."

Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for comment.

The earliest known case in the latest Ebola outbreak involved a health worker in the DRC’s Ituri Province who developed symptoms in late April and later died, though the World Health Organization (WHO) believes transmission may have begun as early as March.

The WHO was first alerted to the outbreak on May 5 after four health workers died within four days. Ten days later, investigators confirmed that the illness was caused by Bundibugyo virus, a form of Ebola.

item.title: Sophie Cunningham sends blunt message to booing, trans flag-waving WNBA crowd after drilling shot
item.description: Portland fans waved a trans flag and booed Sophie Cunningham every touch, but she drilled 3 of 5 from three in the Fever's 112-98 win Friday.

item.title: Property owner advocacy groups push back on Mamdani's 'Rental Ripoff Report,' public database of landlords
item.description: Property owner groups blast Mayor Zohran Mamdani's rent freeze and pied-a-terre tax database, warning small New York City landlords face ruin.
item.content:encoded:
Organizations that advocate on behalf of property owners called out New York City’s democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani in blistering statements to Fox News Digital.

Mamdani campaigned on freezing rents for New Yorkers and appears to have delivered on his crackdown on landlords, upsetting local property owners. He recently released a "Rental Ripoff Report," which makes the case that residents in the nation's largest city are paying too much rent while not receiving enough in return and offers 23 proposals to address the issue.

His administration also sparked controversy by publishing a searchable database identifying affluent property owners who could be subject to the city's proposed pied-à-terre tax, a move critics say could expose them to harassment and public safety risks.

The database, released by the city's Department of Finance, allows users to search properties and view the names and addresses of owners whose non-primary residences could be subject to the proposed tax. A spokesperson for the department said publication of the property roll was required by state law.

MAMDANI WARNING TO WEALTHY NEW YORKERS ABOUT 'FAIR SHARE' SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'FULL BLOWN COMMUNIST'

The Real Estate Board of New York (REBNY) President James Whelan told Fox News Digital that Mamdani was addressing the problem in a counterproductive way.

"The Mayor's report focuses on symptoms, not causes," he said. "New Yorkers are paying record-high rents because there is not enough housing, and many of the reported conditions are concentrated in heavily rent-stabilized buildings that are facing significant operational and financial challenges." 

"Rather than addressing these issues directly, the administration continues to paint property owners with a broad brush, unfairly characterizing an entire industry," Whelan continued. "Seven months into this administration, it is time to prioritize policies that will truly make New York more affordable by increasing housing supply and preserving existing housing."

In response to the searchable database, he warned that many smaller property owners will be caught in the crossfire of what he described as a clumsily directed policy.

"By publishing a database of properties that might be subject to this tax before the tax has even been enacted, City Hall has only added to the confusion surrounding this proposal," Whelan said. "What this database really demonstrates is that the second-home tax is far broader and more complicated than its supporters have suggested." 

"Policymakers should take a hard look at the many homeowners who could be swept in despite not fitting the profile of the ultra-wealthy residents this tax was supposedly designed to target," he added. 

NEW YORK CITY LANDLORDS WARN AMERICAN DREAM IS SLIPPING AWAY UNDER SOCIALIST RENT POLICIES

Ann Korchak, board president of Small Property Owners of New York (SPONY), condemned Mamdani’s influence on politics in a statement to Fox News Digital while discussing his campaign.

"From the start of his mayoral campaign, Mamdani put a target on the backs of property owners," she said. "Small owners are the backbone of the city’s affordable housing stock. We are part of the solution, not the problem, yet he ignores our frontline experience when planning the future of housing." 

"Mamdani repeatedly doubles down on making us the villains, using political stunts like ‘rental rip-off hearings’ and using City Administration officials to go door-to-door to organize tenants while on the taxpayer dime," Korchak continued. "They are not tenant organizers, they’re city officials who represent all New Yorkers — including thousands of small owners."

She added that the hearings were cynical political theater.

"The rental rip-off hearings process was no more independent and objective than last month’s Mamdani-appointed Rent Guidelines Board delivering the rent freeze that the Mayor demanded," Korchak said. "These hearings were political theater to make a case against us. The findings were decided before the hearings concluded, just as the rent freeze was predetermined as we learned from the board member who resigned because of the rigged process."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

She went on to warn that Mamdani’s policies will inevitably punish small businesses and immigrants.

"Mamdani’s housing agenda is stacked against us," Korchak told Fox News Digital. "His rent freeze sets us up for failure. The rents are frozen, but our operating costs and expenses — insurance, utilities, energy, repairs, labor — continue to skyrocket."

"Many rent-stabilized buildings are already at the edge of the economic cliff, and when our buildings fall into disrepair because of his policies, Mamdani will illegally take private buildings from mom-and-pop, immigrant, multi-generational owners and convert them into socialized housing or give them to his hand-picked nonprofit housing providers," she added.

Korchak concluded by warning that widespread damage will be done by his policy agenda.

"Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax is another nail in the coffin," she said. "Creating fear and financial pressure on modest, multi-generational owners, who have poured their life savings, sweat equity and heart and soul into their properties, will destroy the fabric of neighborhoods."

"His list is a database that proves he is targeting property ownership as a whole," Korchak added. "No one is safe."

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s office but did not immediately receive a response.

Fox News’ Amanda Macias, Alec Schemmel, Andrew Mark Miller, and Kiera McDonald contributed to this report.

item.title: Kelsey Grammer admits surprising reason 'Frasier' almost never happened
item.description: Kelsey Grammer reveals a dinner with Paramount's president changed his post-"Cheers" plans and led to the creation of the iconic "Frasier" spinoff.
item.content:encoded:
Kelsey Grammer is revealing the surprising twist that turned "Frasier" into one of television's most successful sitcoms.

The actor recently appeared on "Planet Tyrus," where he revealed he nearly starred in a different show after "Cheers" before one conversation changed everything.

Grammer spent nine seasons portraying the Boston psychiatrist on "Cheers," where the character evolved from Diane Chambers' love interest to one of the bar's most memorable regulars.

KELSEY GRAMMER SUSPECTS HE 'MAY HAVE' LOST HOLLYWOOD ROLES DUE TO CONSERVATIVE VIEWS

"It’s funny, I had visions," the star explained. "I’d been offered another show. They said, ‘We want to do a show with you when "Cheers" is over.’ They said, ‘We think you could actually carry a show on your own.’ I said, ‘Great.’ So we actually started doing it with the same writers that ended up on 'Frasier.' We wrote a completely different story, and they wrote a script. I thought it was kind of funny."

"I went out for dinner with John Pike, who was the president of Paramount at the time," the 71-year-old shared. "... I said, 'Have you read the script?' He said, 'Yeah. And I think a sitcom should be funny. ... This is what you guys have come up with? I don't like it. I think you should play Frasier.'"

"It was John Pike who said, 'Play Frasier.’"

WATCH: KELSEY GRAMMER SHARES THE KEY TO ACHIEVING THE 'AMERICAN DREAM'

Grammer was listening.

"I said, ‘OK, I see what you’re saying. Build an audience. I am kind of funny in the character. He can’t be married anymore, and he can’t have kids,’" Grammer said.

"He did have a son. ... My thing about sitcoms is if there's a child in it, the child growing up every year becomes the most interesting thing about the show. ... Becoming a young woman or becoming a young man is the only really interesting thing that's going on in front of you. So I got rid of that, had him come in once in a while."

Grammer said moving Frasier from Boston to Seattle helped separate the spinoff from "Cheers." It also gave a believable reason why his young son, Frederick, wasn't part of the show full-time instead of making the psychiatrist seem like a "deadbeat dad."

"[I] just had to be a man trying to find his way," said Grammer.

"Whose support payments were on time," Tyrus joked.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"Frasier" premiered on Sept. 16, 1993, and ran for 11 seasons before ending on May 13, 2004. The sitcom won 37 Primetime Emmy Awards and drew 25.2 million viewers for its series finale, becoming one of television's most acclaimed comedies.

In 2023, Grammer reprised his iconic role in the "Frasier" revival on Paramount+, which followed the psychiatrist's return to Boston. The series ran for two seasons before Paramount+ canceled it in 2025.

Noticeably absent from the reboot was John Mahoney, who played Grammer’s on-screen father, Martin Crane. Mahoney died in 2018 at 77.

"John was a remarkably fun guy," Grammer told Fox News Digital in 2021. "He was always kind and sweet and lovely. But the ironic thing about him — when I was directing him once on the show, I said, ‘John, let’s put the dog Eddie in your lap.’ And he says, ‘No, no.’ I said, ‘What’s going on?’ ‘He always bites me. He always growls at me. He scares me, and I don’t like it.’ So I thought, ‘Oh, this is weird. I had no idea.’"

"So they had to put a little sardine oil on his hands, so the dog would lick something instead of trying to growl at him or bite him. This love for Eddie that existed on the show really wasn’t real. It was just an on-camera love. They fought each other, and he was really funny about his relationship with the dog."

"... Every time I spoke to him, we just had a great time," Grammer continued. "We spent time in New York together off-screen, and I saw him in Chicago, and I saw him in Ireland once. He was just a wonderful guy."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

At the time, Grammer said he was eager for what the future held, both personally and professionally.

"You know what? Life always inspired me," he said. "Life and the variety of experience is what inspires me. People inspire me; I love people. I mean, it’s odd that I ended up on a show that was based in a bar. My favorite places on Earth are bars. I’ve had the best experiences, met the most interesting people in bars around the world. And so, what keeps me going personally is that there is always another experience I haven’t known."

"... I'll go right up to the edge before it starts to get dangerous," he joked. "But I love it. I love riding horses, I love shooting guns, I love just exploring all the things that people can do and all the things that a character can do and show you. By virtue of the fact that you've played it, you've actually kind of lived it."

item.title: BROADCAST BIAS: Networks go from hiding Fauci diaries to defending him from Republicans
item.description: Anthony Fauci's diary revealed cozy dinners with Jake Tapper and texts from George Stephanopoulos, but broadcast networks acted as his defense lawyers.

item.title: Florida mail carrier accused of snatching pets on route, trapping 100-plus cats and dogs in ‘hoarding’ house
item.description: A Florida mail carrier allegedly kept more than 100 animals in feces-filled cages with no air conditioning, and now owners are lining up for pet reunions.
item.content:encoded:
The "worst animal hoarding case" a Florida sheriff has ever seen is now expanding as more animals are being recovered.

Some of the rescued animals already have been reunited with owners who said they’d given up hope of ever seeing them again.

Gail Giustino, a 77-year-old mail carrier, was arrested July 20 after authorities found more than 100 animals held in feces-filled cages in her Stuart home. She’d been "collecting cats" she found along her mail route, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said.

RIDGLAN FARMS RESCUE BEAGLES FIND NEW LIFE HELPING VETERANS OVERCOME WAR TRAUMA WITH PAWS OF WAR

With no air conditioning or ventilation, the home was "probably 110 degrees" on the late July day when the animals were removed, Budensiek said in a news conference on July 20 outside Giustino’s home.

"We were coming out here thinking maybe 15, 20, 30 cats," he told reporters, as people wearing white hazmat suits carried out cages holding dozens of cats and at least a dozen small dogs. There was "a foot of animal feces" in parts of the house, Budensiek said.

Some of the caged cats were held fast in feces that had hardened like concrete. Staffers had to smash bricks of feces from around the cats’ legs to allow them to move, Sarah Fisher, spokeswoman for the Humane Society of Treasure Coast, told Fox News Digital.

"When we cracked the door…the stench was unreal," Budensiek said. "The air was stifling hot." He went on to say, "She never walks the pets. She never brings them outside of the house. They've been confined to that animal jail really for however long she's been hoarding these pets."

PARTNER OF WOMAN KILLED BY DOGS RECENTLY SAVED NEIGHBOR WOUNDED IN SIMILAR ATTACK: COURT RECORDS

Investigators faced an "overwhelming" smell of "animal urine, feces, and ammonia," an odor that wafted outside the house, authorities said. The "deplorable" conditions inside the house left "no safe path of entry due to excessive debris, animal feces, and urine," investigators reported.

The odor inside the residence was so severe that it "presented a potential health hazard to responding personnel," arrest records show.

Since 2014, local animal control had issued "up to 65 civil citations" to Giustino for the conditions she’s kept animals, the sheriff said.

DOG SAVED FROM ISIS BY ARMY VETERAN 'KIDNAPPED' FROM FAMILY YARD BY LOCAL AUTHORITIES

And code enforcement officers helped her add air-conditioning units, Budensiek said. But investigators found that those units were not working. And "we haven’t been out here checking on her for the last 10 years," he said.

Giustino could have been charged with up to 160 counts of animal cruelty, Budensiek said. Instead, she was charged with one misdemeanor count of animal cruelty and one misdemeanor count of confinement of animals without sufficient exercise. She was released on a $50,000 bond.

"We truly believe that Gail thinks she's doing the right thing," he said. "But she's doing it the wrong way."

He said, "The goal of arresting her was to be able to seize the animals, to save them from death and try to get them the help that they need."

They also hoped the process would lead to mental health treatment for Giustino, he said. She did not respond to a request for comment by Fox News Digital.

Giustino started working for the U.S. Postal Service in 1997 and is still employed, said Debra Jean Fetterly, a USPS spokesperson for South Florida.

"We are aware of the situation," Fetterly told Fox News Digital. "The Postal Service does not publicly discuss personnel matters."

Days after the arrest, Martin County officials were able to trap and bring in three of four cats that escaped during the rescue effort at Giustino’s home.

And a friend surrendered five more small dogs Giustino allegedly left in her care, Fisher said. By July 29, the humane society had received 108 animals from Giustino’s home.

"We unfortunately are anticipating more of Gail's animals to be coming in the coming weeks" from her friends’ homes, Fisher said. "The sheriff's looking into that right now."

"We don't know really what to expect, but we're prepared."

Meanwhile, staffers have struggled emotionally, she said, because the animals "were in pretty terrible shape."

"They were really just shut down. Some of the cats were catatonic; they wouldn't even move. They were traumatized."

But now, they’ve started showing signs of healing.

"It's actually filling our hearts right now because they have been coming out of their shells," Fisher said. "These cats that weren’t even lifting their heads up are now meowing and seeking attention, and I think they know they're safe."

The 12 tiny dogs recovered from Giustino’s home showed signs of improvement faster, she said.

They were thin, flea-covered, missing hair because of neglect, and were suffering with dental disease, Fisher said. They range in age from 2 to 8, she said, and many appear to be Yorkshire terriers, also known as Yorkies.

"Dogs are just different," Fisher said. "They were happy as could be. They knew they were saved and they were happy. … It's really giving us hope at the shelter."

Further bolstering spirits is the enthusiastic support from locals, Fisher said.

They’ve flooded the shelter with requests to adopt the neglected animals. They’ve brought pizzas, pastries and other treats for workers.

"It’s been beautiful to see," she said.

A big part of the project involves trying to arrange for reunions with potential owners.

On Friday morning, July 24, hearts overflowed with hope outside the shelter.

Dozens of people from all walks of life queued up in the blazing Florida heat, all waiting to see if their missing pets were among those rescued.

"We had 50-plus people, very, very eager right when the doors opened at 10 o’clock," she said.

"They were very wonderful and patient. And one by one, they were all walking out crying because their animals weren't with us."

Shelter employees had hoped for joyful reunions.

"There were grown men crying; there were kids crying. It was so emotional," Fisher said. "It was really, really hard."

By the end of that Friday, two more pet owners rejoiced over their unexpected reunions.

And staffers hope there will be more in the coming days as word spreads about the recovered animals, she said.

Any of the dogs and cats not claimed eventually will be available for adoption. There’s no timeline yet for that.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"We want to make sure that any of these owned animals are going to be going home with their owners, and we're not accidentally going to be adopting them out."

Linh Nguyen called her reunion with 6-year-old Patchy a clear answer to prayer.

SEND US A TIP

He’d disappeared from her yard in early January.

"I’d been praying for his return for seven months," Nguyen told Fox News Digital.

GOT A TIP?

As she prayed, she said she told God she knew it was just "a little thing, just a cat."

But her faith told her that anything was possible.

She posted fliers offering a $5,000 reward for Patchy’s return. She rode her bike through the neighborhood late at night calling his name until she was hoarse. And she kept praying.

"If You do a miracle and bring my cat home," she pleaded in faith, "I will tell everyone it is You."

Then she saw a news report about the rescued cats. She had a strong feeling her missing pet might be among them. And when she stepped into the Humane Society, he saw her right away, she said. She heard meowing that got progressively louder.

"I couldn’t see him, but I recognized his voice."

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Now, Nguyen said, Patchy is thriving at home again and is enjoying walks on a leash.

She’s relieved to know that others are being reunited with their pets, she said. And she’s glad to know that Giustino "will get the help that she needs."

"This," Nguyen said, "is a pure miracle."

item.title: Skin condition under the eyes goes viral as doctors warn it could signal hidden health issue
item.description: Doctors reveal how low ferritin levels in the body can cause dark under-eye circles, pale skin and fatigue even as they warn against self-treating an iron deficiency.
item.content:encoded:
Dark under-eye circles may be more than a cosmetic concern. Doctors say they can sometimes signal low iron stores — a condition that's gone viral on social media under the name "ferritin face."

Experts say there's some truth behind the trend — with important caveats.

Ferritin can be thought of as the body's "iron storage vault," according to Dr. Josef Hadeed, a double board-certified plastic surgeon at Hadeed Plastic Surgery in Beverly Hills, California. It is a protein that stores iron inside the body's cells and releases it when needed.

LOW TESTOSTERONE? HEGSETH SPARKS CONVERSATION AS DOCTORS REVEAL WARNING SIGNS EVERY MAN SHOULD KNOW

"When ferritin levels drop, the body struggles to produce hemoglobin, which is the iron-rich protein within your red blood cells that transports oxygen to the tissues," Hadeed told Fox News Digital.

Low iron levels can compromise skin elasticity, which can make the tissue appear thinner and less resilient, the doctor said.

When hemoglobin is low, the skin can lose its healthy color and appear pale, making the naturally darker tissue beneath the eyes more noticeable, Hadeed noted.

Besides pale skin and dark under-eye circles, other symptoms may signal that someone is lacking iron.

CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS

"The severity of these symptoms generally increases as ferritin decreases," Dane Thomas, a Texas-based hematology/oncology physician associate who specializes in the care of patients with hematologic disorders and cancer, told Fox News Digital.

Low energy, fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, headaches, fainting, brittle or thin nails, hair loss, cravings to chew ice, and restless legs syndrome are a few signs, according to Thomas.

"Some patients also experience decreased exercise tolerance, difficulty concentrating or shortness of breath with exertion," he said.

Other symptoms can include pounding or "whooshing" in the ears, a sore or smooth tongue, rapid heartbeat, intolerance to cold and poor sleep, according to the American Society of Hematology.

Beyond cosmetic concerns, ferritin face may signal an underlying medical condition, including chronic bleeding, gastrointestinal disorders or cancers, or malabsorption, according to hematological experts.

With the rise in bariatric surgery, more patients are developing iron deficiency due to impaired iron absorption, Thomas said. Certain over-the-counter acid-suppressing medications, including proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and H2-receptor blockers, may also contribute to low iron.

While treating iron deficiency is important, identifying and addressing its underlying cause is equally critical, he said.

"Whenever possible, I work with my patients to determine why their iron deficiency developed so we can reduce the likelihood that it will recur," Thomas told Fox News Digital. "This often involves collaboration with gastroenterologists, gynecologists or other specialists to evaluate for sources of blood loss or malabsorption."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Pregnancy, heavy menstrual bleeding and frequent blood donation can also contribute to lower iron levels. Vegetarians, vegans and those who follow diets that do not include iron-rich foods may also be at risk, according to the American Society of Hematologists.

If a person thinks they may have low ferritin, it is important to see a physician.

"This is not something that someone should self-treat, and I always advise them to seek professional help," Hadeed advised. "Unlike water-soluble vitamins, the body has no easy mechanism to excrete excess iron, and over-supplementation can lead to increased levels of iron in the body, which can affect the liver and heart."

A simple blood test by a healthcare professional can determine iron levels. Further evaluation may include stool and urine tests to look for blood, along with endoscopy to examine the esophagus, stomach and colon. Women may also undergo a gynecological evaluation, according to experts.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Treatment for iron deficiency may include oral supplementation and, in cases of severe anemia, intravenous (IV) iron or blood transfusions.

"The biggest drawback of oral iron is gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort and stomach upset," Thomas noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"These side effects can often be minimized by taking iron every other day rather than daily, a strategy that also maintains excellent absorption for many patients."

He also recommends spacing them apart from calcium supplements, dairy products and antacids, which can affect absorption.

Following a diet that includes iron-rich foods can also help, according to the American Society of Hematology website.

Some examples include beef, pork, or lamb; organ meats like liver, chicken, turkey, duck and fish (especially shellfish, sardines and anchovies); leafy greens, such as broccoli, kale, turnip greens and collard greens; legumes, including lima beans, peas, pinto beans and black-eyed peas; and iron-enriched pastas, grains, rice and cereals.

Ferritin face is reversible, Hadeed emphasized. 

Once iron stores are safely restored and hemoglobin levels rebound, the skin recovers its healthy capillary flush, and dark under-eye circles tend to fade over several months.

item.title: WWE SummerSlam 2026 Night 1 preview, predictions and more
item.description: CM Punk defends the Undisputed WWE Championship against Cody Rhodes while Brock Lesnar faces Oba Femi inside a Hell in a Cell at SummerSlam Night 1.
item.content:encoded:
SummerSlam is one of the biggest WWE premium live events of the summer and, for the second straight year, the show will be held across two nights starting on Saturday.

This year’s SummerSlam takes place at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis – the home of the NFL’s Minnesota Vikings. The show will begin at 6 p.m. ET on both Saturday and Sunday nights and multiple championships will be defended over the course of the weekend.

WWE fans can watch the show on ESPN Unlimited.

Read below for a preview and prediction for each match.

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON FOX NEWS DIGITAL

==

It’s the old school going up against the new school in a six-woman tag team match. The Bellas and Paige will take on Fatal Influence. Reid and Henley captured the women’s tag team titles from Brie Bella and Paige at Saturday Night’s Main Event. Now, with Nikki Bella back in the fold, an epic grudge match is set for SummerSlam.

Prediction: Fatal Influence takes care of The Bellas and Paige.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

==

LA Knight is still among the most popular wrestlers on the WWE roster and for the second time, he finds himself in a six-man tag team match on a major premium live event. Instead of teaming with the Usos, he’s going up against them. Knight, Solo Sikoa and Royce Keys go up against The Bloodline. Jacob Fatu and The Usos’ attempts to bring Sikoa back to the family have proven feeble thus far. Sikoa has made clear he wants no part of The Bloodline. Knight has been at war with The Bloodline for years while Keys has been dragged into the fight. He knows Fatu better than most and is itching for a fight.

Prediction: The Bloodline takes care of Knight, Sikoa and Keys.

==

Liv Morgan told Fox News Digital earlier this year she was "everyone’s dream match." Whether that was true for Iyo Sky has yet to be seen. Morgan gets her first Women’s World Championship title defense against the Queen of the Ring. Sky won the tournament at Night of Champions, defeating Morgan in the final and then choosing her as her target. Morgan has been the champion since defeating Stephanie Vaquer at WrestleMania 42. The question will be whether she has any ring rust going into the match against Sky.

Prediction: Iyo Sky returns to the top of the women’s division.

==

Nick Aldis was a decorated world champion before injuries forced him toward a different role. He hasn’t appeared in in-ring competition since he was with Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA), which was then-called Impact Wrestling. But his feud with Gunther will culminate in his first match in nearly three years. Gunther has continuously accused Aldis of dropping the ball when it came to him and putting him off to the side. Gunther maintains he’s the best superstar on SmackDown but hasn’t been treated like it. It all came to a head at Night of Champions when Gunther attacked Aldis backstage. The two have been fighting ever since and Aldis was given the green light to fight Gunther at SummerSlam.

Prediction: Gunther wins a hard-fought match.

==

Oba Femi put off his King of the Ring title opportunity to take on Brock Lesnar in the trilogy fight. Lesnar upped the ante when he said the match would take place in a Hell in a Cell. It’s going to be one of the biggest fights of the weekend and could very well steal the show. Femi could very well slay "The Beast" one final time. Lesnar could prove that he still has it and never lost a step.

Prediction: Femi wins and gets into the world title picture.

==

The tension between CM Punk and Cody Rhodes had been palpable even before WrestleMania 42 when the two champions met in the ring on the go-home SmackDown show. While they were more friends than enemies then, things exploded Friday night when the two men finally exchanged blows. Punk became the champion when he knocked off Sami Zayn for the title and ended his reign after nine days. Rhodes was pinned by Zayn and decided to take his own shot at Punk’s title. Their rivalry finally returns to a WWE ring on Saturday night with the Undisputed WWE Championship on the line.

Prediction: Punk retains the title

item.title: World Series champion Joe Girardi reveals what he finds most 'disturbing' about politics today
item.description: World Series champion Joe Girardi said politics now separates the United States in a way it never did before, calling the shift "disturbing."
item.content:encoded:
World Series champion Joe Girardi revealed what is most "disturbing" to him about politics today.

Girardi, 61, has been in clubhouses for a long time as both a player and a manager. He played 15 seasons in the major leagues as a catcher and then managed for nearly 14 years. The All-Star catcher talked about the difference in politics from then to now.

"I think politics unfortunately has become a hot button for the United States of America unfortunately and it separates us — before where I felt it didn't separate us. That's the most disturbing," Girardi told Fox News Digital in a recent interview.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

The former New York Yankees manager said there were "absolutely" more conversations in the clubhouse about politics toward the end of his time in the dugout than at the beginning of his career.

He said that as a manager, he would tell players to listen to each other.

"I would just tell guys to be patient and listen to each other and understand that you're going to have different views and just be respectful. I mean, you don't have to have the same view. We all grew up different. That's the bottom line, different backgrounds. And just be patient with each other," Girardi said.

WORLD SERIES CHAMPION JOE GIRADI REVEALS THE TWO MAJOR THINGS IMPACTING THE TRADE DEADLINE

Girardi, who won three World Series as a player during his 15-year career and one as a manager of the New York Yankees, said he doesn’t think politics becomes an issue within a clubhouse.

"I don't think it really becomes a problem in too many clubhouses because I think there's a common goal and they find a way to come together with a common goal and that's to win," Girardi told Fox News Digital on behalf of Perfect Game.

Girardi spent the first four seasons of his career with the Chicago Cubs, the next three with the Rockies, the next four with the Yankees and returned to the Cubs for three years before spending his final season with the Cardinals. He made the All-Star Game in 2000 with the Cubs.

He had a career .267 batting average with 36 home runs and 424 RBI. After his playing career, he became a manager. He spent one season with the Miami Marlins in 2006 and then managed the Yankees for 10 seasons, beginning in 2008. Girardi most recently managed the Phillies for 2½ years from 2020 to 2022.

item.title: Savannah Guthrie makes desperate plea six months after mom Nancy went missing: 'Someone knows something'
item.description: Savannah Guthrie's desperate plea reveals her family's six-month agony as Pima County releases ransom notes demanding $4 million in bitcoin.
item.content:encoded:
NBC "TODAY" co-host Savannah Guthrie made a desperate plea for the public's help in a Saturday morning social media post, exactly six months since her mother Nancy was reported missing.

"This is our beautiful Mom. Six months ago, someone took her out of her bed in the dead of night. We have lived every moment, every breath, and every heartbeat in agony and despair ever since," Guthrie wrote to open her Instagram message.

"Every day, we wake up and try to be strong and go on - because that’s what our joyful and resilient Mom taught us to do," she continued. "But make no mistake - our hearts are in ruins. Cam and Kristine, Annie and Tommy, Mike and me - we spend every waking moment thinking of her, longing for her, looking for her."

"There is a hole inside us that can never be filled," Savannah wrote. "There is an ache that cannot be softened. And there is a determination in us that cannot be quenched - to find out what happened to her, so that we can give her the dignity of a proper goodbye - a celebration of her remarkable life that she so deserves."

NEW DETAILS FROM NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM DEMAND REVEALED, 'HER LIFE IS IN YOUR HANDS': REPORT

Guthrie's early morning post came just one day after the Pima County Sheriff's Department released a pair of ransom notes Friday in the hopes that someone might recognize the documents' "unique linguistic style."

"We are begging for help. We are desperate," Savannah's post continued. "We need someone to come forward. Someone knows something. Someone suspects something. Someone recognizes the writing in the ransom demand notes."

"Someone has noticed something different, strange, troubling or just unusual - perhaps with someone they deeply love," she wrote. "Perhaps they are afraid to come forward. Perhaps they are conflicted. Perhaps they are angry or upset for being in this situation. There is a way out - to tell what you know. You can do so anonymously. The reward is available. There is a way to end this situation and do the right thing."

"We are real people, facing real grief, doing the best we can, and counting our many blessings along the way - most especially the prayers and love from good people, which we feel deeply. We need your prayers, we need your kindness. We need the good to be stronger than the evil. If you are following this story for entertainment or for profit, you are not on her side - you are part of the harm perpetrated against her. We will never stop looking for answers - and we will never stop looking for the light. We will always be hoping and praying and believing in the best of our world - in spite of circumstance. This is what our faith makes possible. Please. Bring her home," she concluded.

NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTES DON'T MATCH SUSPECT'S BEHAVIOR, PROFILER SAYS: 'I DON'T BELIEVE THEY'RE REAL'

The 84-year-old Nancy Guthrie was last seen outside her home in the Catalina Hills near Tucson, Arizona, on Jan. 31.

The home's doorbell camera recorded a masked intruder disconnecting the cameras at approximately 1:47 a.m. local time on Feb. 1.

At 2:28 a.m., her pacemaker lost its Bluetooth connection to her cell phone, according to the Pima County Sheriff's Department.

The newly released ransom notes, which the sheriff's department said were sent on Feb. 2 and Feb. 6, demanded a ransom of $4 million to be paid in Bitcoin, while the author threatened to kill Nancy Guthrie.

The notes included references to the crime scene that may not have been public at the time they were sent — including details about the location of Guthrie's Apple Watch and the smashed floodlight in her backyard. Fox News Digital first learned about the watch on the morning of Tuesday, Feb. 3. According to authorities, the note had been sent the day before, on Monday, Feb. 2, indicating the sender knew about it before the information began to seep out into the public sphere.

NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTE CLAIMED THAT SHE HAD DIED, BEEN ‘BURIED WITH NATURE,’ SOURCE SAYS

The second note claimed that Nancy Guthrie had "perished."

Fox News Digital contacted the Pima County Sheriff's Department for further comment.

Fox News Digital's Michael Ruiz contributed to this report.

item.title: The dinner candle you're actually supposed to eat as restaurants chase memorable experiences
item.description: A South Florida entrepreneur invested over $20,000 to launch edible candles with a patented formula, now targeting restaurant tables nationwide.
item.content:encoded:
A South Florida entrepreneur believes the next big innovation in entertaining isn't another kitchen gadget or smartphone app. It's a candle you can eat.

Claudia Mosley, founder of CeraViva, has created handcrafted edible candles that melt into warm dipping sauces and dessert spreads, transforming an ordinary meal into what she calls "an experience."

"The product is not really the candle," Mosley told Fox News Digital. "The candle is the vehicle. The product is the experience that you're giving your guests."

CHEF WHO FLED COMMUNIST COUNTRY OPENS WORLD'S FIRST MICHELIN-STARRED CUBAN RESTAURANT

Made with organic and premium ingredients, the candles are designed to pair with bread, vegetables, seafood, meats or desserts, Mosley said.

Savory flavors include chimichurri, shrimp scampi and parmesan cream, while sweet varieties include raspberry cream, apple pie and a new Key lime pie flavor.

Mosley said her sweet candles contain no added sugar.

AMERICA'S MOST-SEARCHED ICE CREAM BRAND MAY SURPRISE YOU — AND THERE'S A HEALTHY REASON WHY

"They're sweet, but they're not super sweet," she said. "They have the perfect balance."

Each candle is crafted to encourage people to put away their phones and spend time connecting around the dinner table, Mosley said.

The business represents more than culinary creativity for Mosley. Born in Colombia, the 50-year-old mother of four immigrated to the United States as a teenager and built a successful merchant services company with her identical twin sister before launching CeraViva.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Mosley said she's been living the "true American dream."

That entrepreneurial mindset has shaped every step of the venture. Mosley said she has invested more than $20,000 to launch the business, obtaining the necessary state licenses, moving production into a commercial kitchen and developing a patented formula designed to withstand shipping and refrigeration.

Consumers can purchase the candles directly from CeraViva's website for $38, but Mosley said her bigger goal is getting them onto restaurant tables.

"Every restaurant is looking for an experience," she said.

Diners would order the edible candle as an appetizer before their meal, giving it 20 to 25 minutes to melt into a warm dipping sauce while they talk, she said.

Mosley's edible candles are meant to create conversation, encourage families to unplug and give restaurants a memorable experience customers can't get at home.
